enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal dismissed after alleged non-receipt of hearing notice
key_facts: A Turkish asylum seeker appealed against refusal of asylum but neither returned a Reply to Directions nor attended a first hearing.
The adjudicator dismissed the appeal without considering its merits under rule 33(2)(a), relying on deemed service of the hearing notice.
The claimant and his solicitors said they never received the notice; the Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal without resolving that assertion.
Wilson J held that where non-receipt is credibly asserted, dismissal without merits is unlawful and leave should be granted if the assertion has a real prospect of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal against an adjudicator's non-merits dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed; leave application remitted for fresh consideration; Secretary of State ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appellant credibly asserts that a procedural notice was never received, the Immigration Appeal Tribunal must weigh that assertion and grant leave if it has a real prospect of being true, because dismissal without considering merits is not lawful where there has been no relevant failure to comply with a direction.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of dismissing an asylum appeal without considering merits under rule 33
Effect of deemed service under rule 48(2)(a) when non-receipt is asserted
Whether the Tribunal may ignore an assertion of non-receipt
Relationship between overriding objective of just disposal and individual justice

enrichment.short_title: TOLATA sale of family home after residence order reversal

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Former cohabiting parents were beneficial joint tenants of the family home at 74 Laughton Road, Northolt.
The mother initially sought deferred sale under TOLATA; after a residence order was made to the father, each party reversed position and the judge ordered immediate sale.
The father's Schedule 1 Children Act application was adjourned and risked dismissal while the TOLATA claim proceeded alone.
The Court of Appeal upheld the sale order but criticised failure to hear competing TOLATA and Schedule 1 applications together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a county court order for sale under section 14 of TOLATA.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; order for sale upheld despite identified procedural and reasoning flaws.
enrichment.ratio: Under TOLATA section 15 the court has a power, not a duty, to order sale and must have regard to specified factors including children's welfare; where co-owners invoke TOLATA and Schedule 1, case management should normally conjoin the applications so neither statutory regime prejudices the other.
legal_issues: Whether TOLATA replaced the section 30 duty-to-sell approach
Construction of 'intentions' and 'purposes' in section 15(1)
Weight of section 15(3) circumstances and wishes in a dispute between equal beneficiaries
Overlap between TOLATA and Children Act Schedule 1 applications

enrichment.short_title: Speed camera conviction challenge on fresh grounds
key_facts: The appellant was convicted by magistrates of driving at 36 mph in a 30 mph limit on the A443 at Hallow.
Before the magistrates he relied on section 89(2) and lack of corroboration; on appeal to the High Court he advanced a new point about Speedmaster DS3 cross-check markings.
Magistrates had found the automatic camera accurate, certificated, and self-corroborating through dual readings.
Owen J held the new challenge raised issues not explored below and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated or equivalent application to the High Court against magistrates' conviction for speeding.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal against a speeding conviction based on a prescribed device, a party cannot reopen factual issues that were not raised or explored before the magistrates, including conditions of Secretary of State approval under section 20 of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988.
legal_issues: Admissibility of evidence from prescribed speed detection devices
Section 89(2) single-witness opinion rule
Whether new grounds about device operating conditions could be raised on appeal

enrichment.short_title: IGPA pepper contracts and defective declaration of shipment
key_facts: Indonesian sellers sold Muntok white pepper C&F to European buyers under IGPA contract form no. 5.
Goods were loaded on unpowered barge INTAN 6, declared shipped, then lost when the barge sank off Bangka Island.
Buyers refused documents; the IGPA Board of Appeal held declarations naming the barge were defective because INTAN 6 was not a first class ship.
Following P.T. Putrabali v Fratelli de Lorenzi, the court held declarations valid in form and remitted for damages assessment after sellers compromised Singapore cargo claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal with permission against two IGPA Board of Appeal arbitration awards.
enrichment.outcome: Awards set aside; appeals remitted to the Board of Appeal for assessment of damages and determination of counterclaims.
enrichment.ratio: Under IGPA form 5 clause 10, a declaration of shipment is judged by form and timing rather than underlying performance; failure to object within three business days renders a declaration effective, and buyers may reject C&F documents only where non-conformity appears on their face without further investigation.
legal_issues: Validity of declaration of shipment naming an unpowered barge
Whether clause 6 requires shipment on a contractual vessel before declaration
Effect of buyers' failure to object within three business days
When shipping documents may be rejected under C&F terms
Measure of damages after sellers compromised subrogated cargo claims

enrichment.short_title: Restrictive covenant tied to Cadogan settled estate
key_facts: In 1929 the Sixth Earl Cadogan sold land including 60-62 Chelsea Manor Street to Chelsea Borough Council with a covenant restricting use to housing the working classes.
The covenant was expressed to benefit adjoining land only while it remained part of 'the Cadogan Settled Estate in Chelsea'.
The 1889 settlement was dismantled in 1961 and the benefited land ceased to be settled land.
Dano Ltd sought to develop the site as private housing; the Court of Appeal held the covenant unenforceable once the settled estate ended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a declaration that no benefited land remained within the covenant's scope.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; covenant held spent and unenforceable.
enrichment.ratio: Where a restrictive covenant is enforceable only while benefited land 'forms part of the Cadogan Settled Estate in Chelsea', the word 'settled' refers to the settlement existing in 1929 and the covenant cannot survive dismantling of that settlement even if Cadogan family interests continue in neighbouring land.
legal_issues: Construction of 'Cadogan Settled Estate in Chelsea'
Whether covenant benefit survives reorganisation of the Cadogan estate in 1961
Purposive versus literal interpretation of estate-described covenant benefit
Impact on Peabody Trust affordable housing lease

enrichment.short_title: Warsaw Convention costs after Part 36 payment in

statutes_considered.title: Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules Relating to International Carriage by Air (Warsaw Convention as amended at The Hague 1955)
Carriage by Air and Road Act 1979

key_facts: Cargo was destroyed when a Korean Air B747 crashed near Stansted on 22 December 1999.
Claimants sued for high-value helicopter gearbox and printing press cargo losses subject to Warsaw Convention weight limits.
Korean Air offered limit-based settlements but paid slightly more into court in July 2002, which claimants accepted.
Morison J held Article 22(4) did not bar costs because the payment into court exceeded the last written offer within six months of commencement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by carrier for an order depriving cargo claimants of costs after acceptance of payments into court.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; claimants entitled to costs under Part 36.
enrichment.ratio: Article 22(4) of the Warsaw Convention deprives a claimant of costs only where damages awarded do not exceed a qualifying written carrier offer made within the prescribed period; where the payment into court exceeds that offer, the exception does not apply and CPR Part 36 costs consequences operate without conflict.

Whether acceptance of a payment into court constitutes an award of damages
Conflict between international convention and CPR Part 36
Conversion of SDR limits to sterling for payments into court

enrichment.short_title: Council tax disaggregation in blind care home
key_facts: Kathleen Chambers House in Burnham-on-Sea is a purpose-built RNIB residential care home for blind and partially sighted residents.
The listing officer sought to disaggregate four two-person units for separate council tax assessment while 32 single-person units remained aggregated.
The Valuation Tribunal allowed RNIB's appeal, finding no cogent distinction between disputed and non-disputed units.
Mitting J quashed the tribunal decision for flawed reasoning and remitted to a freshly constituted tribunal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court against a Valuation Tribunal decision on council tax disaggregation.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a new Valuation Tribunal; listing officer ordered to pay £4,000 towards RNIB's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Whether part of a building is a 'self-contained unit' under Article 2 of the Council Tax (Chargeable Dwellings) Order 1992 is a single objective question to be answered in light of all circumstances including the purpose for which the building was constructed; subjective developer intent and comparison with the listing officer's treatment of other units are irrelevant.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'self-contained unit' in Article 2
Whether communal care-home facilities negate separate living accommodation
Irrelevance of subjective builder intent and actual use
Two-step versus holistic approach to disaggregation

enrichment.short_title: Albanian asylum claim and state protection for domestic violence
key_facts: An Albanian woman claimed asylum based on fear of violence from her former partner and his family, including after her father's murder in Albania.
The Secretary of State refused asylum and certified the claim as not raising a Convention reason.
A Special Adjudicator dismissed the appeal after a preliminary finding of sufficient Albanian state protection for victims of domestic violence under Horvath.
The IAT refused leave to appeal; Harrison J dismissed judicial review, holding the Adjudicator's assessment was balanced and not Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal against dismissal of asylum and human rights appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; leave to appeal refusal upheld; costs ordered against publicly funded claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Sufficiency of state protection under Horvath must be assessed in light of the claimant's particular feared harm, not domestic violence in Albania generally; where objective material shows legal frameworks, police training, and support services, a balanced conclusion that protection meets the practical Horvath standard is not perverse even if victims must initiate prosecutions themselves.
legal_issues: Horvath test for sufficiency of state protection against non-state actors
Whether protection analysis may be decided as a preliminary issue
Relevance of victim-initiated prosecution in Albania
Whether police laxity shows unwillingness rather than inefficiency
Certification under paragraph 9(4)(a) Schedule 4

enrichment.short_title: Contributory negligence for seat belt and drunk driver
key_facts: A 16-year-old back-seat passenger suffered serious head and other injuries when the defendant's car hit a railway bridge after speeding and drinking.
She was not wearing a seat belt that was available but not readily accessible under the back seat.
The judge found the head injury would have occurred even with a belt but other injuries would not, reducing damages 15% for the belt and 10% for accepting a lift from a drunk driver.
The defendant's renewed application for permission to appeal challenged expert findings and departures from Froom and Owens guidelines.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against contributory negligence apportionments in a county court personal injury trial.
enrichment.ratio: Trial judges may apportion contributory negligence separately by injury type where effects can be distinguished; reductions below Froom and Owens benchmarks may be justified by age, limited seat-belt availability, and the claimant being led by older companions, and such assessments will rarely be disturbed on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Green belt gypsy caravan very special circumstances

statutes_considered.title: Planning Policy Guidance Note 2: Green Belts (PPG 2)

key_facts: Mrs Porter, a gypsy with serious ill-health, sought retention of a residential mobile home at Willow Tree Farm, Iver, in the green belt after years of unlawful occupation.
A planning inspector found very special circumstances in personal hardship and lack of alternative pitches, overriding green belt policy.
South Bucks District Council challenged the decision under section 288; the Secretary of State conceded quashing on precedent grounds but the judge upheld the permission.
The Court of Appeal quashed the permission for failing to analyse unlawfulness of occupation and broader Chapman-compliant planning context.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against dismissal of a challenge to a planning inspector's appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; inspector's grant of permission quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Very special circumstances justifying inappropriate green belt development require clear and cogent analysis in the planning context, including the unlawfulness of long-standing breach of control and the gypsy/non-gypsy comparator question highlighted in Chapman; a mere catalogue of personal hardship without that broader reasoning is insufficient.

Relevance of unlawful occupation under Chapman v United Kingdom
Precedent as a ground for refusing green belt permission
Application of section 54A and PPG 2 paragraph 3.2
